inclusion_rule: At least 1000 GitHub stars, claims to reduce or improve context for coding agents, and pushed within the last 6 months.
notes: Stars are a maintenance signal, not a quality signal. In measurements so far they have been anti-correlated with retrieval quality: codesearch (72 stars) beats graphify (109k stars) at tight token budgets.
tier drives execution order. 'light' loads no model and is safe to run in batch. 'heavy' loads an embedding model or a service and MUST run last, one at a time, behind the probe's memory guard.
Local embedding tools are pointed at LM Studio's OpenAI-compatible endpoint rather than Ollama, using the already-present text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5.

candidates.claim: typed graph over code, docs, SQL schemas and configs
candidates.tier_behaviour: The most size-robust arm measured. 56.8% at 4k on gin (99 files), 35.4% on fastify (300), 30.1% on hugo (932), answering every case at every size bar one. It loses absolute recall as repositories grow — everything does — but without the reliability collapse seen elsewhere.

candidates.claim: zero-server local graph on LadybugDB
candidates.entry_point: gitnexus index, then gitnexus context <query> (bin lives in the gitnexus/ workspace package)
candidates.note: Earlier reading of the monorepo root package.json found only gitnexus:refresh/gitnexus:full and wrongly concluded there was no query surface. The CLI is in the gitnexus/ workspace package (bin.gitnexus -> dist/cli/index.js) and exposes index, context, cypher, impact, embeddings and detect-changes. A graph retriever with a real ranked-context command.
candidates.result: Best 16k-budget recall in the entire field at 60.8%, and last among real tools at 1k (2.4%), because it spends a 16,385-token median payload to get there. 0/76 failures, 14.8 s median latency, 13.9 s / 1,678 MB per index. The clearest single example of why this benchmark reports three budgets instead of one.

candidates.entry_point: MCP search tool (to be confirmed at probe)

candidates.claim: benchmarked context reductions on reviews and large-repo workflows
candidates.note: Builds fine — 110 files, 1,630 nodes, 18,010 edges — and `search` returns JSON with status/query/search_mode/summary/results/confidence. But the results carry entity and symbol names with no file paths, so it cannot be scored as a file retriever from this entry point. Its `query` or `detect` subcommands may expose locations; not yet explored. Flags to know: --repo not --path, --embedding-provider must pair with --embedding-model, and `search` accepts no --data-dir.

candidates.claim: LSP-backed semantic retrieval; find_symbol and find_referencing_symbols over 30+ languages
candidates.note: Works once the language server is installed: on Go it needs gopls, and without it find_symbol fails outright. Its ide-assistant context exposes NO search_for_pattern and no semantic search of any kind — the retrieval surface is LSP symbol lookup only, scored via find_symbol with substring matching on the most distinctive query token. Coverage is gated on per-language toolchain installs, a cost no other mechanism here carries.

candidates.claim: context window optimization for AI coding agents
structural AST pattern search; matches code shape rather than text
candidates.note: Working at 0.45.1. No prose entry point, so each query token is fed as a literal AST pattern and matches are unioned.

candidates.claim: BM25 plus dense vectors over AST-chunked code
code health, generated docs, git analytics via MCP
candidates.note: Works, but `init` generates a full wiki per invocation. Because each case is indexed at its own base revision, a 76-case corpus needs 76 wiki builds and the run did not finish in 4.5 minutes on that arm alone. Needs a per-repo shared index to be benchmarkable; scored on a subset instead.

candidates.claim: uses 99% fewer tokens
candidates.note: Best performer measured. On gin: 44.0% at 1k, 75.1% at 4k, 75.8% at 16k, zero failures, 631 ms, 3,848 tokens. Its "99% fewer tokens" claim measures as 94.6% fewer than the git-grep baseline (3,848 vs 70,681) while delivering HIGHER recall at every budget above 1k — the first headline claim in this field that roughly holds up. Indexes lazily on first search; no service required.

candidates.claim: self-hosted search for humans and agents
enterprise-grade 40m+ LOC codebase intelligence, zero setup, local
faster grep; baseline class rather than a context provider
candidates.note: Built from source at 7.8.4. Working. Its --include rejects a brace list; -O<ext> is the correct file type selector.

candidates.claim: light-weight embedded AST-based code search CLI
candidates.note: The published wheel does not declare sentence-transformers, so `index` aborts out of the box with "No module named 'sentence_transformers'". Installing it with `uv tool install --with sentence-transformers` fixes it completely: gin indexes to 109 files / 1,168 chunks (957 go, 209 markdown) at 77.6 MB peak RSS. A one-line dependency omission was the entire barrier.
candidates.result: 5.7%/21.9%/27.5% at the 1k/4k/16k budgets, r@10 26.9%, 5,196-token median payload, 0/76 failures, 937 ms median. Clears the null controls (2.6% random, 1.8% churn at 4k) by a wide margin but sits well below the leaders, at 0.04 recall per 1k tokens. Answers every query, which several better-scoring arms do not. A 3-case smoke of this same arm read 0.0%; the 76-case figure is the real one, which is the argument against publishing anything off a handful of cases.

candidates.claim: cut AI token costs 95%+ on code exploration
candidates.note: Its MCP surface is only six generic tools; retrieval is one of 91 catalog actions dispatched through `order` and discoverable via `menu`. `repo` is the registered repository name, which is the basename of the indexed directory, so per-revision worktrees work if named deterministically. Results are returned as interned file IDs (@1, @2) with a separate path legend rather than as paths — a path-regex adapter scores it 0% recall while it is in fact returning correct symbols.

candidates.claim: trigram index; the engine behind Sourcegraph search
candidates.note: Working and measured. Two gotchas: it indexes with a separate binary (zoekt-index, flag -index) and queries with zoekt (flag -index_dir); and it has no -num flag, which silently failed all 76 cases on the first attempt. Given a whole prose string it treats the input as a phrase expression and returns almost nothing, so queries must be issued per token.
candidates.tier_behaviour: Indexed gin (99 files) and scored 8.2% at 4k, then failed to index on all 111 medium-tier cases across fastify (300 files) and hugo (932). Recorded as did-not-index rather than as poor recall, which is the distinction that matters: it is not retrieving badly at this size, it is not running.

candidates.claim: 97% reduction in Claude Code input tokens, 27.5% lower API cost, 100% local
candidates.note: Builds and installs (33 MB Go binary) but hard-requires Ollama at localhost:11434 with nomic-embed-text. Its init offers an OpenAI provider, which an OpenAI-compatible local server could satisfy, but the default path fails with a connection error to Ollama. Its claimed "97% token reduction, 27.5% lower cost" is therefore unverified here.

candidates.claim: coding agent focused on efficiency and context curation
candidates.note: Pre-screen found 22 browser-open references. Described as a coding agent focused on context curation — an agent, not a queryable retriever. Excluded before install rather than after disrupting the machine, which is what the pre-screen exists for.

candidates.claim: universal AI context generator; saves thousands of tokens per conversation
give your repo a brain
candidates.note: Full command set is init/version/ask/refresh/doctor/report/log-decision/clean. There is no retrieval command: `init` injects static context files into .repobrain/ and `ask` is an LLM Q&A wrapper over them. Mechanism is orientation-map plus generation, not retrieval, so it has no comparable ranked-result surface. Excluded from scored arms on mechanism, not on quality.

candidates.claim: local-first semantic code search engine
candidates.note: Works — returned the correct file for a test query — but cannot be benchmarked per revision. Its seagoat-server daemon binds to one repository path and indexes asynchronously: after 90 seconds on gin it still reported 15,315 queued chunks with no ready signal, so any query races a partial index. Per-revision scoring would need a server restart and full reindex per case. Same incompatibility class as repowise. Also downloads a 79 MB all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ONNX model from S3 on first run.

candidates.claim: hybrid vector plus BM25 over tree-sitter chunks, fully offline
candidates.note: Below the 1000-star bar but retained: current accuracy leader at tight token budgets, and evidence that stars do not predict quality.
candidates.availability_note: Its binary is no longer present on the measurement machine, so the medium tier could not include it and the small-tier figures (48.2% at 4k over four repos) cannot currently be re-derived. Needs reinstalling before the small-tier numbers are republished.

candidates.claim: standalone Aider repo-map with personalized PageRank
candidates.note: Fails the 6-month freshness rule (257 days) and is broken by tree-sitter drift, but works pinned to tree-sitter 0.25.2. Included for coverage with both facts recorded. Personalization needs identifier names, not prose: fed identifiers it ranks the correct file first, fed prose it scores below random.

candidates.claim: structural code context for verification-backed review
candidates.note: Best recall-per-token in the field at 5.86 per 1k tokens, 12x the next provider, on a 68-token payload. Two blockers: it cannot index a 1,461-file repository because a snapshot is 248 MB and 101,053 nodes against its own MAX_IMPORT_BYTES of 32 MB and MAX_IMPORT_NODES of 100,000; and it serves phantoms on 72% of stale-index cases. Measured on the same public corpus as every other provider.
candidates.measurement_caveat: Now measurable through product code: a headless bin drives extract::BundledTreeSitterEngine, interchange::export_json and query::search_page — the same call sequence api.rs uses, minus DB persistence and the Tauri progress emitter. No module needed widening; the bin plus a Cargo.toml entry were the only additions.
candidates.scaling_limit: The 32 MiB MAX_IMPORT_BYTES ceiling binds far earlier than a file count suggests. Measured snapshot sizes: gin 17.8 MB (56% of budget, 123 files indexed), fastify 29.5 MB (88%, 379 files), then hugo 128.8 MB, fastapi 104 MB, nest 122 MB and django 480 MB all REFUSED. At 1.9-3.6 KB of snapshot JSON per node, 32 MiB buys roughly 9k-17k nodes, i.e. about 150-400 indexed files. MAX_IMPORT_NODES (100,000) is effectively unreachable: only django exceeds it, and it breaches the byte limit ~15x first. So the arm is structurally confined to the small tier, and the earlier framing of the wall at 1,461 files was too generous.
candidates.ceiling_mechanism: Explains the flat budget curve (36.1/39.1/39.6%): recall is capped by hit count, not by the requested node limit. On gin the query 'Add fullPath in context copy' returns 23 hits across just 6 distinct files at node_limit=400 with truncated=false. After per-file dedup there are not 20 files to fill a 16k budget, so extra budget buys nothing.
candidates.cheapest_headroom: export_json uses serde_json::to_string_pretty while import checks json_text.len(), so about 35% of the import budget is indentation whitespace. Compact encoding of the identical graph is 0.64-0.67x (gin 17.8 -> 11.4 MB, fastify 29.5 -> 19.7 MB). Not changed here; it is the shipped format.
candidates.tier_behaviour: Measured across three sizes through product code. gin (99 files): 36.1/39.1/39.6% on a 68-token payload, reproducing the old fixture figures exactly. fastify (300): 12.7/17.6/20.3% on 2,520 tokens — recall halves and payload grows 37x, so the recall-per-token advantage that made it notable (5.86 per 1k on gin) collapses to 0.07 on fastify and is a small-repo artifact rather than a property of the tool. hugo (932): refused on all 29 cases, snapshot 128 MB against a 32 MiB ceiling. Usable ceiling is roughly 150-400 indexed files, so it does not reach the top of the medium tier.
candidates.RETRACTION: Every CodeVetter figure published before 2026-08-23 is understated. The adapter sorted the graph's ranking descending while the query returned an ascending match-rank, so recall was measured over the worst-ranked results. Corrected, the same pre-change binary scores 27.1% rather than 17.6% at a 4k budget on fastify. The scale now runs 0..=999_999 higher-is-better, so the adapter's descending sort is correct as written and must not be 'fixed' back to ascending.
candidates.result_after_improvements: Re-measured 2026-08-23 against an improved binary (sub-token indexing, IDF field-weighted scoring, saturation fix, preview trimming) with the adapter sort bug corrected. Case-weighted over 154 cases on 4 private repos: 52.3% / 53.7% / 53.7% at 1k/4k/16k on a 687-token median, versus graphify 36.0% / 52.8% / 53.7% on 1,780. Wins r@1k on all four; ties at 4k for a third of the payload. The curve is flat by construction: it delivers everything within 1k tokens.
candidates.capacity_correction: An earlier entry here claimed a capacity defect on site-health. That was my error: I measured HEAD (110 files, 3.7 MB) and reasoned about historical revisions. Cases are scored at base_revision, and site-health's median case revision has 537 code files and a 65.3 MB snapshot because a monorepo was extracted out of it partway through its history. Only 20 of 86 revisions fit under 32 MiB, and those refusals are legitimate scale, not a defect. The 150-400 indexed-file envelope stands; I had retracted it wrongly.
candidates.real_defect_found_and_fixed: The 0%-recall-when-answering case WAS a genuine defect, with two causes. extract_sql scanned every line of every metadata text file for the bare words from/join/into/update, so "extracted from Fleet Workspace" produced a table named Fleet; it is now gated on an unambiguous multi-word SQL marker. And structured config contributed nothing searchable: a 183 KB projects.json produced 9 nodes, none carrying keys or values, so any question about a config file's contents had only the path to match and scored structurally 0 at every budget. config_entry nodes now cover json/jsonc/yaml/toml/ini plus named dotfiles, with lockfiles skipped, uninformative values collapsed, and a 400-entry-per-file cap. On site-health's 20 fitting revisions: r@1k 11.7% -> 55.0%, zero-hit 85% -> 30%. Net snapshot cost about nil since removing the SQL noise pays for the config coverage; prose-heavy repos got smaller (got -8.1%).

candidates.entry_point: ts use <path>, then ts search [--semantic] <pattern> --limit N
candidates.note: Indexes gin's 120 files in 0.11s, the fastest build in the field, and caches into <repo>/.token-savior so a worktree collects its own index. Regex `search` works out of the box and searches non-code files too, which will cost it precision on a code-retrieval corpus. `--semantic` needs two dependencies the wheel does not pull: sqlite-vec, then fastembed. Both are recoverable and the tool names them in its own error text.
candidates.measurement_caveat: Run with --no-daemon so nothing outlives the harness. Measured per call, that costs ~57 s of CPU at 454 MB RSS: without the daemon the semantic index is not persisted, so each query re-embeds the whole repository rather than merely reloading the model. Its latency here is therefore a hard worst case and should be read as 'cold, no daemon', not as what a warm agent session sees — the daemon exists precisely to amortize this. Recall and token cost are unaffected, since the embeddings computed are the same either way. The symbol-level lexical index is separate and genuinely cheap at 0.11 s.
candidates.result: Semantic mode: 15.1% recall on a 25-token median payload, the smallest in the field and the highest recall-per-token (6.05). Returns scored symbols with signatures and docstring heads, never file bodies — useful for an agent that will open files itself, weak for one that will not. 3/76 unavailable.
candidates.second_arm_result: Regex mode, scored as a separate arm because it is a different mechanism: 29.4%/52.3%/52.3% on a 1,914-token median payload with 0/76 failures. It out-recalls the semantic mode by 3x at a 4k budget for 75x the tokens, and it indexes non-code files, so CHANGELOG hits are expected and are charged for.

candidates.entry_point: cgc index <path>, then cgc find content <token> (COLUMNS must be wide)
candidates.note: The earlier note saying Neo4j was wrong: its own doctor reports `Using database: falkordb`, and the documented embedded option (`pip install falkordblite`) is unsatisfiable against the package's own pins. A FalkorDB container works instead — port 6379 was already taken on this machine, and FALKORDB_PORT in ~/.codegraphcontext/.env redirects it cleanly. Once connected it is the strongest graph builder measured here: 1,323 Function nodes on gin in 42.9 s at 1,176 MB peak, with 8/8 tree-sitter parsers probing OK including Go. Contrast code-graph-rag, which produced zero symbol nodes on the same repository. Its .env also references ANTHROPIC_MODEL for graph queries, so whether its retrieval surface is LLM-mediated needs confirming before it can be scored as a peer of the non-LLM arms.
candidates.external_service: falkordb (default) — not neo4j; a container on any free port works
candidates.result: Verified by hand: indexing a gin worktree takes 33.2 s and `cgc find content fullPath` then returns 20 matches including the `Copy` and `FullPath` functions in context.go — the exact ground-truth file for that case. Its graph is the richest measured here at 1,323 Function nodes. Two integration details were found and fixed: the output is a Rich table that wraps each absolute path across four lines unless COLUMNS is forced wide, and the graph is shared across every repository ever indexed, so each case must delete its own worktree or later cases search a graph containing earlier revisions of the same files. Even with both fixed, the 76-case harness returns a 93-token 'no matches' payload per case while the identical command sequence works standalone. Cause not identified. Deliberately NOT recorded as 0.0% recall: by this benchmark's own rule a zero is a claim about the instrument until the provider's bytes have been read, and here the bytes say the tool works. Left as unresolved rather than published as a number.

candidates.entry_point:
cgr daemon up, then cgr start --repo-path

--update-graph --capture all, then cgr start --ask-agent (LLM) or cgr mcp-server
candidates.note: Provisions its own Memgraph and Qdrant via `cgr daemon up`, which is the smoothest service setup of any candidate here. Indexing gin takes 3.07 s at 760 MB peak. Two things put it outside the comparable set on this corpus, both measured rather than assumed. First, the resulting graph contains no code symbols on a Go repository: node types are File, Folder, Package, Project and ExternalPackage only, and `--capture all` (groups: structure, calls, types, imports, io) changes nothing — the file count only doubles because a second project joins the shared Memgraph. Second, its natural-language surface is `--ask-agent`, which requires orchestrator and cypher *models*, so it retrieves by having an LLM write Cypher. That is a different mechanism from every other arm and would measure a model plus a graph rather than retrieval. Its MCP server enumerated zero tools over stdio in two probes. Minor: an unknown subcommand such as `cgr language list` surfaces as a full Python traceback (NoSuchCommand) rather than a usage message.
candidates.external_service: memgraph + qdrant (milvus is an optional extra, not required)

candidates.entry_point: gortex daemon start --detach, then gortex track <path>, then gortex context --task <prose> --index <path> --token-budget N --format json
candidates.note: The only provider in the registry that accepts an explicit --token-budget, which is the axis this benchmark had to invent in order to compare the rest — every other tool is measured under a budget it was never told about. Takes the task in prose via --task, so no query rewriting. Indexes gin in 2.30s at 44 MB peak, the cheapest real index measured. Returns callers grouped by file, with paths relative to the repo's parent, so each one arrives prefixed with the repo directory's own name. The 317 MB binary is the cost: it statically links the go-sitter-forest grammar set.
candidates.setup_requirement: A daemon must be running before any query. `track` only writes config — it does not index and does not start the daemon — so a track-then-query sequence with no daemon fails every call with "no gortex daemon is running" and a usage dump. This cost a full 76-case arm scored at 0.0%/100% unavailable before the cause was found; the tool names the fix in its own error text.
candidates.result: 76/76 answered, no failures. 39.5%/55.5%/55.9% at the 1k/4k/16k budgets on a 888-token median payload — the best recall-per-token of any arm whose absolute recall is competitive (0.62). Its 17.6 s median latency is the daemon indexing each fresh worktree on demand, which a long-lived repo would pay once rather than per query.
candidates.tier_behaviour: Degrades monotonically with repository size, and the failure mode changes as it goes. gin (99 files): 55.5% at 4k, every query answered. fastify (300): 21.6%, and 29 of 82 queries returned nothing at all while still reporting zero failures — visible only because outcomes are tracked separately from accuracy. hugo (932, Go): 11.8%, with 11 of 29 cases failing to index inside a 5-minute per-call timeout. Its daemon also grew from 14.7 MB to roughly 2.5 GB across about 110 repository indexes, and individual queries were observed running past 30 minutes before the timeout existed. Strong on small repositories, unreliable by the medium tier.

candidates.note: Zig build with no zig compiler present on this machine, and references Postgres besides. Two installs deep before it can be measured, so it goes last.

candidates.entry_point: repowise init, then repowise search <query> --mode hybrid --limit N --format json
candidates.note: AGPL-3.0, ~6.2k stars, one of the largest projects in this category. It was WRONGLY absent: the earlier blocked-egress exclusion applied to the separate `repowise-npm` package, which references api.repowise.ai and ships a custom licence. This project documents 'self-hosted, runs on your machine, the first index needs no API key' and 'source never leaves your network', and that held on test. Telemetry is opt-out and was disabled before measuring. Index cost 7.47 s at 331 MB peak on gin.
candidates.mechanism_note: Distinct from every other arm: `init` generates a wiki (222 pages on gin) and `search` queries those pages, so retrieval runs through generated documentation rather than over code directly. Results still carry real source paths and line numbers, so it remains comparable on the same metric. Offers fulltext/semantic/symbol/concept/path/hybrid modes; hybrid is measured as its own recommended blend.
candidates.also_publishes_benchmark: repowise-dev/repowise-bench, with pre-registrations and raw data, graded against CodeGraph, codebase-memory-mcp, Graphify and code-review-graph — overlapping this registry. Their headline question is call-edge precision, not retrieval recall, so the two are complementary rather than contradictory. Worth reading as an independent cross-check.

BLOCKED: `index` aborts with 'No embedding provider configured' and requires a .chunkhound.json config, so the documented key-free regex path is not reachable — with no index, `search` then fails with 'Database not found'. Recoverable by pointing it at a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which would make it a semantic rather than a regex measurement; recorded rather than worked around.

candidates.note: The maintained upstream of the repo-map mechanism. The registry already holds pdavis68/RepoMapper, a standalone port of exactly this, blocked on a stale dependency — while the 48k-star original was absent. Note the recorded finding that repo-map scores poorly on prose queries applies here too.

Russ Cox trigram indexer and direct ancestor of the registered zoekt. Regexp-only, so it joins ast-grep in the no-prose-entry class. Last pushed 2025-05-29, which fails the six-month freshness rule. Recorded because the registry previously held a DIFFERENT 72-star project also called codesearch.
Packer, not a retriever: recall is 1.0 by construction because it returns the whole repository. Already covered by the repomix-pack-all and repomix-compressed control arms.

inclusion_policy.principle: Maximum coverage. Nothing is dropped for being an awkward fit; every candidate is scored on the entry point its own documentation recommends for finding task-relevant code, and that entry point is recorded per candidate.
inclusion_policy.rationale: Excluding a tool for interface mismatch hides it; scoring it on the wrong entry point misrepresents it. Recording the entry point does neither. This also prevented two errors already: repo-map scored 11.1% when fed prose instead of identifiers, and ast-grep has no prose entry at all.
inclusion_policy.category_mismatch_handling: Reported as a flag beside the number, not as an exclusion. A packer's recall is 1.0 by construction and a pattern matcher needs a pattern; both are stated rather than hidden.
inclusion_policy.only_remaining_exclusion_axis: Source egress. Tools that upload the user's proprietary code to a third party are held back pending an explicit per-tool decision, because that is a privacy choice rather than a methodological one.

baselines_and_controls.note: Not products, so not candidates. Listed so the registry total is not mistaken for the arm count.

discovery.note: The registry was originally assembled from recall, which cannot tell a reader whether a tool is absent by judgement or by oversight. This sweep re-derived the field from GitHub keyword and topic search and found 34 repositories above the star floor that recall had missed, of which these were in scope. Rerun it before publishing: the category is moving fast enough that the longlist goes stale.
discovery.known_flaw: FIXED 2026-08-23. Four independent failure modes, only one of which had been identified: (1) the diff matched on the tail of owner/name, so same-name-different-owner collided — this recurs for repowise, codesearch, octocode, codegraph, claude-context and semble, so it is the common case; (2) it read `candidate.repository` while the registry stores `repo`, making that half of the dedupe dead code and silently falling back to id matching; (3) --limit 50 on best-match ordering meant a query like 'code graph' filled its slots with name-matching repositories and never reached the 67.7k-star largest member of the category, which also carries no topics at all; (4) the 1,000-star floor cut against this benchmark's own finding that stars are anti-correlated with retrieval quality, since fully-local members sit at 84-533 stars. Now: full-slug matching, both schema keys, 16 topics, limit 200, floor 200, and bare-id matches surfaced as needs-verification rather than treated as covered.

dimensions.external_service: Whether the provider needs a database or container running beside it. Not a quality signal, but it decides who can actually adopt the tool, and it is the single biggest reason a candidate in this registry went unmeasured. Values seen: none, neo4j, milvus/qdrant, postgres, redis.
